h.select_rule: Discard any hypothesis whose condition is the edited field's own current value, or whose condition merely disables or disconnects the edited component. From the rest, keep 10 with distinct mechanisms and field pairs, favouring those where an informed expert could plausibly bet on either direction.
h.strategy: Two patterns are banned because experts find them obvious: (1) conditioning on the current value of the same field being edited, which just restates that upgrading a weak setting helps more than upgrading a strong one; (2) conditions that make the edited component unused, unreachable or inert. Instead, each hypothesis must link two DIFFERENT fields that interact through a non-trivial mechanism, such as substitution between parallel routes, a capacity already supplied elsewhere, one part acting as a bottleneck for another, or interference that turns a usually helpful edit harmful. No condition setting may appear in more than two hypotheses. Use the gaps and negated assumptions as the source of each idea. In each 'why', name the mechanism and explain why the opposite direction is also a priori plausible.

hyps.why: At high learning rates, larger batches damp the gradient noise that drives instability, whereas elsewhere the lost steps dominate.
Under standard parameterization wide nets take larger function-space steps per update, so raising the learning rate destabilizes them first.
Strong L2 on every layer compounds multiplicatively across depth, collapsing signal through the added layer.
When width is the capacity bottleneck, an extra layer supplies missing expressivity that wide nets do not need.
Wide nets carry the most surplus capacity, so added L2 removes excess fit rather than useful fit.
sklearn divides the L2 term by the minibatch size, so tiny batches amplify the effective penalty and raising alpha over-regularizes.
Large batches leave few steps in the epoch budget, so a larger learning rate is needed to converge.
Large updates compound through stacked ReLU layers, so adding a layer at high learning rate destabilizes training.
With few optimizer steps, the harder-to-train deeper net cannot reach its potential within the epoch budget.
At tiny learning rates wider nets move further in function space per Adam step, converting width directly into faster fitting.
